claims.text: The starting catalyst is a nearly equiatomic multi-element automotive alloy containing transition metals and minor platinum-group elements.
The starting catalyst's surface sites are susceptible to deactivation through sintering.
The starting catalyst is susceptible to corrosion and platinum-group-metal loss.
Thermal aging and exposure to H2O and NO deactivate the untreated catalyst.
Atomic layer deposition at approximately 150–200 °C can apply an ultrathin, conformal high-entropy spinel oxide coating to the catalyst.
Controlling ALD cycle count and precursor chemistry can preserve coating porosity and active-site accessibility.
The ALD intervention produces a uniform, nanometer-thick high-entropy spinel oxide layer.
The oxide layer acts as a physical barrier against sintering and corrosion.
The oxide layer promotes optimized adsorption and desorption of intermediates on dynamically formed active sites.
The coating suppresses undesirable surface segregation.
High configurational disorder in the coating enhances the flexibility of adsorption and desorption kinetics for species such as OH and NO.
Protection from corrosive attack reduces platinum-group-metal loss.
The coated catalyst will have higher catalytic activity than the untreated catalyst during transient, low-temperature exhaust operation.
The coated catalyst will have greater durability than the untreated catalyst under H2O, NO, and thermal cycling.
The coating will sustain catalytic performance while maintaining low platinum-group-metal consumption.
Performance benefits depend on precise ALD optimization that avoids excessive active-site blocking.
The protective effects may diminish under extreme operating conditions or suboptimal coating parameters.
Literature on high-entropy oxide coatings and ALD processes supports the proposed mechanism.
